events.title: Borland Delphi 1.0 launched
events.summary: On February 14, 1995, Borland launched Delphi 1.0 — a drag-and-drop Windows app builder that compiled to fast native programs.
events.about: Delphi combined Pascal with a visual form designer: drag buttons and grids onto a window, double-click to write code, compile to a fast Windows .exe. Thousands of business apps — database screens, reporting tools, inventory systems — were built with it in the 1990s. Anders Hejlsberg's team later moved to Microsoft and shaped C#.

narrative.whyChosen: Delphi proved you could build Windows apps as quickly as Visual Basic but get C++-class speed in the finished program.
narrative.whyImportant: It kept Pascal alive for a decade of GUI development and influenced later rapid-development tools and C#.
narrative.problemSolved: Windows developers wanted Visual Basic's ease of building screens, but needed faster runtimes and reusable UI components for serious business software.

events.title: Ada 95 standardized
events.summary: ISO published Ada 95 on February 15, 1995 (ISO/IEC 8652:1995) — the first major revision of Ada with object-oriented programming, protected types, and child units.
events.about: Ada 95 modernized the DoD systems language for avionics, rail, and safety-critical software: tagged types, hierarchical libraries, and improved real-time support. It remained the default where compilers must prove absence of runtime surprises — Boeing, Airbus, and nuclear systems.

narrative.whyChosen: Ada 95 brought OOP to the safety-critical language mandated for US defense projects.
narrative.whyImportant: It kept Ada relevant for embedded and certification-heavy domains through the 2000s.
narrative.problemSolved: Ada 83 lacked modern abstraction; mission-critical systems needed safer OO without C++'s footguns.
